1:
Where the passage belongs and when it was spoken they leave open. Gill says it is not certain whether this followed the offerings of the princes, and reports a Jewish view that God spoke in the night, because then the lamps were burning. Henry observes that directions for the candlestick had been given long before, and made according to the pattern shown in the mount, but only now were the lamps ordered to be lighted, when the other furniture began to be used. Calvin says plainly that this precept, like many others, is not inserted in its proper place. Keil's block here is almost wholly verse quotation, adding only that the choice of the Levites in place of the first-born has been noticed already.

Which way the lamps threw their light is worked out two ways. Ellicott gives the architecture: the candlestick stood against the south wall opposite the table of shewbread, its seven branches running east and west, so that the lamps threw their light northward, by which the holy place was more effectually lighted than had the candlestick faced the entrance with its branches north and south. Wesley reaches the same position from the shewbread table on the north and the candlestick close to the boards on the south, so that the lights fell on both sides of the sanctuary. Calvin gives a different reason: God would have the lamps set opposite the candlestick so that the brightness of the gold might shine over against them, and the very stand of the light retain its beauty.

Whether the verb means to light or to set up Ellicott alone raises, correcting the rendering twice; the others take it of the lighting, and Wesley describes how it was done, the middle lamp kindled from the fire of the altar and the rest one from another, signifying that all light comes from Christ, who has the seven spirits of God figured by the seven lamps of fire. Who was to do it Gill discusses, reporting that the office was not incumbent on a high priest alone but belonged to the common priests too, and supposing Aaron did it himself only because this was the first time; in which, he adds, Aaron was a type of the great High Priest who lights the lamps in all his golden candlesticks, the churches. Henry makes the act doubly representative: as the people's representative to God Aaron did the office of a servant, lighting his Master's candle, and as God's representative to the people he gave them the intimations of his will and favour.

On the candlestick Ellicott corrects three renderings: the clause describes the material rather than the workmanship, the gold was turned or twisted rather than beaten, and the two limits named are literally its base and its blossom, the whole from bottom to top. Wesley presses the word the other way, that the gold was not hollow but solid, beaten out of one piece and not of several joined together. Clarke turns the whole to emblem: the candlestick stands for the Church of Christ, the oil for the graces and gifts of the Spirit, the light for those gifts in action among men, so that God builds his Church and sends his Spirit to dwell in it that it may be shown to the world as his own workmanship; and the seven lights point to the seven Spirits of God, seven denoting among the Hebrews anything full, complete and perfect. Gill notes the fitness of the moment, that God having taken up his residence in the most holy place and the sacrifices having begun outside, the service of the holy place should be set on foot too, since neither shewbread nor incense could be attended to until the lamps were lighted. Calvin marks that Aaron is expressly said to have obeyed, as if in no despicable matter.
5:
Who officiated at the cleansing they answer two ways. Ellicott says that as Moses had already officiated at the consecration of the priests, so now, though Aaron and his sons were already consecrated, he is commanded to officiate at the Levites' cleansing. Calvin makes the opposite point: lest the Levites arrogate more than was right, God anticipates their presumption three ways, by deferring their consecration, by desiring that they should not be initiated by Moses but by Aaron, and by appointing a different ceremony; had they been initiated with the priests they might have contended to be on an equality with them. Gill agrees that the cleansing was Aaron's work, in which he was a type of Christ, the refiner and purifier of the sons of Levi.

What the water of purifying was none of them settles. Clarke reads it as water of sin, made from the ashes of the red heifer with cedar-wood, hyssop and scarlet, her blood sprinkled seven times, so she may be reckoned a proper sacrifice for sin; the ashes kept ready at hand he calls a concentration of the essential properties of the sin-offering, available with little expense or trouble, and typifying, as Hebrews shows, the blood of Christ. Wesley agrees on the ashes and infers that the ordinance was prescribed before though mentioned after, such transplacings of passages being frequent in scripture. Ellicott is more cautious: no explanation of the particular water is given, the same word covers the bullock at Aaron's consecration and the Levites' own sin-offering below, and he thinks the reference probably to the brazen laver, allowing only that some unrecorded direction about the ashes may lie behind it, in which case the sin-offering must have preceded the sprinkling.

The shaving and washing they take as sign. Wesley says the rite signified the cutting off of their inordinate desire of earthly things and the singular purity of heart and life required in the ministers of God. Calvin reads the razor as the putting off of the flesh, that they may begin to be new men, and the washed clothes as diligence lest any impurity be about them; then Aaron offers them like the holy bread or incense, that they should acknowledge they were no longer their own masters. Ellicott stays with the words: literally cause the razor to pass over all their flesh, a weaker word than that used of the leper's cleansing, and the Levites, not brought into such contact with the holy things as the priests, were required only to wash their clothes, the ordinary preparation for worship.

Taking the Levites from among the children of Israel divides them furthest. Calvin makes it a subtraction from the number of the people, and turns on the Papal clergy, who under this pretext claim immunity to live as they like in exemption from the laws, not only an unsound deduction, he says, but one full of impious mockery, since the ancient priesthood attained its end in Christ and the succession they allege robs Christ of his right. Gill takes it more quietly of separation to their work as ministers to the priests: they had been mixed among the tribes before the journey from Sinai, and as Aaron did not assume the honour of priesthood to himself, so the Levites did not take the honour of their office to themselves. Henry draws the rule, that all employed for God must be dedicated to him according to the degree of employment: Christians must be baptized, ministers ordained, and we must first give ourselves to the Lord and then our services. Keil's block is chiefly quotation, adding only that after the purification the Levites were to bring two young bullocks, one with its meat-offering for a burnt-sacrifice and the other for a sin-offering, and that Moses was to bring them into the court and gather the congregation in its representatives.
8:
The bullock they take differently. Gill turns to the rabbis on its age, gathering from the second bullock named next that it was two years old, though the wise men say three years and others allow four or five, the decision going with the wise men. Wesley leaves the age alone and asks why this victim: it is the same sacrifice offered as a sin-offering for the whole congregation, because the Levites came in the stead of all the first-born, who did in a manner represent the congregation. On the bringing near Gill and Keil agree, Gill that they were brought not outside the tabernacle but within it, in the court or at its door where the altar stood, and then to the altar itself, where the Lord was in some sense present to accept the sacrifices; Keil that Moses was to cause them to enter the court, and afterwards to come before Jehovah, that is, in front of the altar.

Who laid on hands all three settle the same way. Wesley says not all the children of Israel, which was impossible, but some in the name of all, the princes or chiefs of each tribe, who used to transact things in the name of their tribes; Keil says the tribe-princes in the name of the Israelites, and that the congregation itself was gathered in the persons of its heads; Ellicott glosses the whole assembly as, here as elsewhere, the representatives of the people.

What the act transferred divides them. Keil argues, against Knobel, that it was not merely a sign releasing them from the possession of the nation, but a symbolical transfer to the Levites of the obligation resting upon the whole nation to serve the Lord in the persons of its first-born sons, presenting them as representatives of the first-born, to serve him as living sacrifices. Ellicott reaches nearly the same place by the language, noting that the phrase is the one used of the offerer laying his hand upon the victim, so that the nation's obligation touching the first-born was transferred to the Levites, and they given over to the priests as the Lord's representatives. Wesley says they signified the transfer of the right of ministering from the first-born, in whose hands it formerly was, and their entire resignation of them to God's service. Clarke alone hears a modern question in it: it has been argued from this that the congregation had a part in appointing their own ministers, and that by imposition of hands; however that may be, he says, what was done here meant no more than that the people gave up the tribe to God in place of their first-born, binding themselves to provide for men who, because of their sacred service, could follow no secular work — for surely they who served the altar should live by the altar.

How the waving was done none will guess confidently. Gill denies that they were actually moved to and fro by Aaron, which he could not do, though he thinks Aaron may have made the motion himself and they the like after him. Wesley says the same, that Aaron caused them to imitate the motion, waving themselves toward the several parts of the world. Keil takes it to have been a solemn conducting up to the altar and back. Ellicott says the manner is not expressed, and offers both possibilities, leading them backwards and forwards before the people, or the waving of Aaron's hands. What it signified they read as belonging and readiness: Gill that they belonged to the Lord of the whole earth; that some think it testified readiness to serve, and that constant employment is figured by the motion, though he reports Ainsworth's supposition that it figures the troubles and afflictions of the ministers of God instead; Wesley that it signified readiness to serve God according to their capacity wheresoever they should be.
12:
What the Levites' own imposition of hands did, Gill and Keil name differently. Gill takes it of transferring their sins to the bullocks, since these were to make atonement for them, and calls it a figure of the imputation of sin to Christ, leading the faith of the offerers to the sin-bearing Saviour; with Aben Ezra he reads the singular head as the head of every one. Keil says that by it they made the animals their representatives, in which they presented their own bodies to the Lord as a living sacrifice well-pleasing to him, closing the transfer with a sin-offering and a burnt-offering.

The setting before Aaron they gloss briefly. Gill, following Aben Ezra, marks that it came after atonement was made, and that they were then presented to Aaron and his sons as their ministers. Wesley adds the direction of the gift: to the Lord they were first properly offered, and by him given to the priests for his service. Ellicott keeps to the rendering: offer them for an offering is literally wave them as a wave-offering. Keil paraphrases the whole run at once: Moses was to place them before Aaron, wave them, and so separate them from the children of Israel that they might be his, after which they should come to serve the tabernacle. Gill sums the separation by listing what effected it: the water of purification, the sacrifices, the presenting before the Lord with the people's hands upon them, the waving, and the setting before Aaron.

Where they were to go in divides them. Gill draws the limit hard: not into the sanctuary, where only the priests entered, much less into the most holy place, where only the high priest went once a year, but into the court of the tabernacle. Ellicott and Wesley let them further: Ellicott into the court to keep watch, to assist the priests at the altar, and to take down and set up the Tabernacle as occasion required; Wesley likewise into the court to wait on the priests, and at present into the tabernacle itself, to take it down and set it up. On the doubled word Gill offers three readings: that given, given is repeated for confirmation; that they were twice given, first to the Lord by Israel and then to Aaron, as Chaskuni; or, with Jarchi, that the two givings answer to two services, the carrying of the vessels and the song.

Calvin alone works the exchange as an accounting problem. Lest the other tribes complain that the people was diminished, God declares the Levites alienated from the race of Abraham, having acquired them when he smote the first-born of Egypt and spared Israel's; but the reason would seem to fail once God, demanding the price of redemption, set the first-born free, else he would require the same thing twice. His solution is arithmetic: the first-born of the twelve tribes exceeded the Levites, so all twenty-two thousand went free of the tribute and God took the Levites in their place, only the two hundred and seventy-three excess being redeemed; God was content with terms so equal as not to oppress the people. The compensation made on one day did not discharge Israel as to children not yet born, so the law of redeeming the first-born was passed for the future; nor was it unfair that Levites' children should be consecrated, since whatever tribe they sprang from they were already his. Given, Calvin adds, means not a gratuitous gift but belonging by compact. Ellicott raises a narrower crux and leaves it open: whether the clause about the first-born is an exact equivalent of such as open every womb or a limitation of it, since an exact equivalent would force on first-born a different sense from the one it commonly bears in the Pentateuch, where it is restricted to the first-born son on the father's side.
17:
What the word gift carries is the first difference. Gill reads it as a second giving, the Lord giving to Aaron and his sons the Levites first given to him, when Israel laid hands on them and they were offered; before that he notes only that God gave up his right in the first-born and took the Levites for his use instead, Clarke adding nothing but a cross-reference on the manner of redeeming the first-born. Calvin denies the obvious sense: by a gift is not to be understood an act whereby a person resigns and cedes his own right to another, but, devoting them to the ministry of the sanctuary, God desires that they should have a leader and master, obeying Aaron's commands.

Why the appointment averts a plague they answer three ways. Ellicott makes it competence: the appointment of the Levites in place of the first-born was calculated to insure the reverent and orderly discharge of the duties of the Sanctuary, and to safeguard against the sins of omission and commission into which the first-born would more likely have been betrayed, which would have provoked the divine wrath against Israel. Wesley makes it guard duty: they were to guard the tabernacle and not suffer any of the people to come near it or meddle with holy things, which if they did would certainly bring a plague upon them. Calvin makes it twofold: they were to be intercessors or ministers of reconciliation, either sense being appropriate, and as guardians of the sanctuary they would keep the Israelites from bringing destruction on themselves by rash approach; whence, he adds, there was no room for ill-will towards them unless the people were annoyed that God had taken measures for their welfare. On the atonement they were said to make, Wesley denies that it was by offering sacrifices, which the priests alone might do, and confines it to assisting the priests in that expiatory work and a diligent performance of all the parts of their office.

Calvin alone turns the inauguration into an argument about Moses. The Levites are inaugurated in their proper order, their condition being inferior; and here, he says, the sons of Moses and their descendants were placed in this lower rank and excluded from all expectation of the priesthood, which makes the later ingratitude of the people, and especially of the tribe of Levi, the more base, when they presumptuously sought the honour from which Moses had shut out his own children for ever. It was no ordinary act of obedience in Moses to execute what God appointed; Aaron is named because he consecrated them in right of his priesthood; and the people's consent is merely commended, a virtue that only increased their ignominy when they later sought to overthrow the decree they had approved.

That the ceremonies did not suffice without atonement Clarke presses hardest: though the Levites had been solemnly consecrated and all legal washings performed, they could not approach God till an atonement had been made, and he wonders that any priest or people should attempt to draw nigh without one, since there is no entrance into the holiest but through the blood of Jesus. Calvin turns the same act forward, taking their presentation by Aaron's hands as a shadowing of what shone out at the coming of Christ, since the prophets had predicted that in the renovation of the Church those hitherto but of the multitude should become Levites: by this figure God would declare that none even of his elect servants would be accepted unless sanctified by the one Priest. Keil stays with the calendar, fixing the Levitical period at twenty-five years and upwards to the fiftieth, after which the Levite returns from the work and only serves his brethren in keeping charge, which as distinguished from work signifies the oversight of the tabernacle furniture rather than laborious service.
22:
On the going in Gill is brief: they entered the court, having stood at its door while the rites of consecration were performed, and the times of entering and leaving were fixed at the same session. Calvin makes the verse the seal of the whole: in the type nothing pertaining to the legitimate service of God was omitted from the ancient priesthood, whose main point is obedience and the purity that flows from it; the Levites served before Aaron because they humbly submitted to the yoke and let themselves be controlled by the will of the priest, since God had so enjoined. He adds that the history will shew how prone man's nature is to rebellion, so that sad conclusions sometimes follow successful commencements.

The age of entry is the difficulty, since an earlier chapter musters the Levites from thirty; Clarke disposes of it by cross-reference, having reconciled the two terms already. Keil argues from the shape of the law: the heading and final clause that bound it, and its position immediately after the induction of the Levites, show that it was binding for all time and meant for their standing service, and so does not clash with the earlier muster from thirty to fifty for the transport. Ellicott offers three possibilities and settles on none: the rule may fix the age of entry after the taking of Canaan, in force until David substituted twenty, once the carrying of the Tabernacle had ceased with the removal of the ark to Zion; or the chronological order, not always observed in this book, may have displaced later directions; or the Levites may from the first have entered the lighter parts of their office at twenty-five and the more onerous, removing the Tabernacle and bearing the sacred vessels as the Kohathites did, only at thirty.

Calvin argues both limits from prudence, not from the text. Had they been admitted in early youth their levity might have detracted from the reverence due to sacred things, since the immature are given to pleasure and intemperance, and by negligence or ignorance might have made grievous mistakes in the service of God; and as they were unfit until they had attained prudence and gravity, so, lest they fail from old age, they were seasonably dismissed, their duties being laborious and demanding bodily strength. He applies it to the pastoral office both ways: none should be chosen but such as have given proofs of moderation, yet those who diligently devote themselves should not be unreasonably pressed, nor more required than their ability can bear, for some foolishly count years, as if it were a sin to choose a pastor before his twenty-fourth.

What the dismissed Levite still did they answer alike. Gill has him give advice, instruct younger Levites and do lighter service, and reports Jarchi that they returned to shutting the doors, singing and loading wagons, objecting that the last seems too burdensome; the charge is watching that no stranger or unclean person enter. Clarke agrees almost word for word: they acted as general directors and counsellors near the camp, singing praises and seeing that none unclean entered; Wesley says only that it was advice and assistance in lesser works. Ellicott draws it as a distinction of kind, between the heavy labour of carrying the furniture and slaughtering the victims and the charge or oversight of the vessels of the Sanctuary; Keil glosses the word as attendance upon an official post; Ellicott renders the service literally of warring the warfare, the fifty-year-old returning from the warfare of the service. Clarke turns the whole to the ministry: if so much legal purity fitted the Levites for their work, no ordinary measure of holiness can fit a minister of the Gospel, and none may expect the kingdom whose heart is not sprinkled from an evil conscience; Antinomianism, he warns, is more general among religious people than is imagined.
